reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC & ACC-AHA guidelines
clinicalPearls: In complete heart block there is no conduction from atria to ventricles, so atrial and ventricular activity are entirely independent, giving AV dissociation with a slower, regular ventricular rate driven by an escape rhythm
The ECG shows P waves and QRS complexes marching independently, with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular rate
The reliability and rate of the escape rhythm depend on its origin: a narrow junctional escape is usually faster and more stable, whereas a wide ventricular escape is slower and less dependable
Presentations include fatigue, breathlessness, presyncope, syncope, and haemodynamic collapse, and it can precipitate cardiac arrest if the escape fails
Common causes are age-related conduction system fibrosis, ischaemia or infarction (particularly inferior), drugs affecting the AV node, and infiltrative or post-procedural disease
Reversible causes such as offending drugs, hyperkalaemia, and ischaemia should be sought and corrected
Symptomatic or high-risk complete heart block is an indication for cardiac pacing, temporary in the acute setting and permanent for irreversible block
In acute inferior infarction the block is often transient and nodal, whereas anterior infarction with block implies extensive damage and a worse prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: Complete heart block arises when conduction through the AV node or the His-Purkinje system is entirely interrupted, so no atrial impulse reaches the ventricles. Ventricular activity then depends on a subsidiary escape pacemaker distal to the block. Block within the AV node typically produces a junctional escape with a narrow QRS and a relatively faster, more stable rate, whereas block in the His-Purkinje system produces a ventricular escape with a wide QRS, slower rate, and greater risk of asystole. Causes include degenerative fibrosis of the conduction system, ischaemic damage, increased vagal or drug-induced nodal suppression, electrolyte disturbance, and infiltrative processes.
additionalDifferentials: Second-degree AV block (Mobitz I and II)
High-grade AV block with occasional conduction
AV dissociation without true complete block
Sinus bradycardia or sinus arrest with a junctional escape
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG and continuous rhythm monitoring to confirm AV dissociation and characterise the escape
Electrolytes including potassium and review of AV-nodal-blocking medications
Assessment for acute ischaemia or infarction including cardiac biomarkers
Echocardiography to assess ventricular function and structural or infiltrative disease
Evaluation for infiltrative, inflammatory, or infective conduction system disease when suspected
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: haemodynamic instability, syncope, or an unreliable slow wide-complex escape rhythm at risk of asystole, requiring urgent temporary pacing
Complete heart block complicating acute anterior myocardial infarction, indicating extensive damage
Recurrent syncope (Stokes-Adams attacks) from transient ventricular standstill
Escape rhythm failure progressing to asystole and cardiac arrest
reference.prognosis: Untreated symptomatic complete heart block carries a high risk of syncope and sudden death, but permanent pacing restores a normal prognosis in most; outcome is worse when block complicates extensive anterior infarction or advanced structural heart disease, and better when a reversible cause is corrected.
pitfalls: Mistaking marked AV dissociation from other mechanisms for true complete block, or vice versa
Failing to identify and reverse causes such as AV-nodal drugs, hyperkalaemia, or ischaemia before committing to permanent pacing
Underestimating the instability of a wide-complex ventricular escape rhythm
Delaying temporary pacing in a symptomatic or unstable patient
management: Identify and correct reversible causes - withdraw atrioventricular-nodal blocking drugs, treat hyperkalaemia and other electrolyte disturbance, and address acute ischaemia
In symptomatic or unstable patients, stabilise with atropine and a chronotropic infusion such as isoprenaline or dopamine while arranging pacing
Institute temporary pacing (transcutaneous then transvenous) for haemodynamically significant block, particularly with an unreliable wide-complex escape
Implant a permanent pacemaker as the definitive treatment for irreversible complete heart block
Provide urgent coronary reperfusion when block complicates acute myocardial infarction
Continuously monitor rhythm and haemodynamics, with defibrillation and resuscitation available should the escape rhythm fail
Assess ventricular function and any structural or infiltrative disease with echocardiography to guide device selection
